CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 30




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                   )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                     )
         FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                        )
         APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA LARGE LOAD                    )
         TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                    )     CASE NO. PUD2026-000046
         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                          )
         CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                   )
         RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                         )
         PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                       )




                                       Redacted Rebuttal Testimony

                                                    of

                                                John Laws

                                               on behalf of

                                   Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company




                                             October 5, 2026
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 30




                                                  John Laws
                                          Redacted Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.    My name is John P. Laws. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.    By whom are you employed and in what capacity?
    6    A.    I am employed by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) as its
    7          Chief Commercial Officer.
    8
    9    Q.    Please summarize your professional qualifications and educational background.
   10    A.    I have over 25 years of experience in executive leadership, with a proven track record in
   11          corporate strategy, corporate finance, and corporate development to include negotiations
   12          with counterparties on matters such as strategic commercial contract arrangements, asset
   13          portfolio construction, capital formation and mergers and acquisitions.
   14                 Most recently, I served as a consultant to OG&E and advised on certain negotiations
   15          with counterparties related to the Company’s power procurement efforts and large new
   16          loads. Previously, I served on the Cabinet of Governor J. Kevin Stitt as Secretary of Budget
   17          and State Chief Financial Officer. In this capacity, I advised Governor Stitt and his
   18          administration on state policy, fiscal strategy, and legislative matters among other duties.
   19                 Prior to that role, I was employed by Enable Midstream Partners, LP, and its
   20          predecessors, where I held several leadership positions, most recently as Executive Vice
   21          President, Chief Financial Officer, and Treasurer. In that role, my responsibilities included
   22          overseeing finance, treasury, accounting, external reporting, internal audit, investor
   23          relations, and risk management functions.
   24                 Prior to Enable Midstream, I served as Director of Corporate Development at OGE
   25          Energy Corp. In that role, I evaluated strategic alternatives for certain assets, developed
   26          business strategies, and negotiated asset acquisitions, including the OU Spirit wind
   27          generation facility and the Redbud combined-cycle gas-fired power plant.
   28                 Earlier in my career, I had experience as a principal investor with Hunt Private
   29          Equity Group, Inc., a Dallas, TX-based private equity firm, where I originated, evaluated,

         Redacted Rebuttal Testimony of John Laws                                              Page 2 of 29
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 30




    1          and executed leveraged buyout and growth capital investment opportunities on behalf of
    2          the firm. I began my career with Arthur Andersen LLP, where my duties included
    3          performing valuation analyses for public and privately-held business interests.
    4                  I earned a Master of Business Administration from the McCombs School of
    5          Business at The University of Texas at Austin and a Bachelor of Business Administration
    6          in Finance from the University of Oklahoma.
    7
    8   Q.     Have you previously testified before this Commission?
    9   A.     Yes. As a witness for OG&E, I previously submitted testimony in Case No. PUD2025-
   10          000038 and Case No. PUD2025-000031.
   11
   12   Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony?
   13   A.     The purpose of my Rebuttal Testimony is to respond to recommendations concerning the
   14          customer protections contained in OG&E’s proposed XLPL Tariff and Terms and
   15          Conditions. Specifically, I first address the overall framework and the appropriate use of
   16          comparisons to other large-load tariffs.      I then address proposals concerning CIAC;
   17          contract term and renewal; termination and capacity-reduction fees; collateral; Preliminary
   18          Agreements; and late-payment provisions. I explain why OG&E’s proposed protections
   19          are reasonable, administrable, and necessary to protect existing customers from the
   20          financial risks associated with serving extra-large loads, and I identify limited clarifications
   21          that OG&E does not oppose.
   22
   23                                 OVERVIEW AND FRAMEWORK
   24   Q.     Does OG&E believe that the provisions contained in the XLPL Tariff and Terms and
   25          Conditions provide significant customer protections to other rate classes?
   26   A.     Yes. As explained in Direct Testimony, OG&E used its successful negotiations with
   27          Google and the terms contained in the Google ESAs as the foundation for the XLPL Tariff
   28          and Terms and Conditions. OG&E also designed the XLPL Tariff and Terms and
   29          Conditions to be consistent with HB 2992’s requirements, including a separate large-load
   30          tariff, a long-term service commitment, adherence to cost-causation principles, revenue



        Redacted Rebuttal Testimony of John Laws                                                 Page 3 of 29
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 30




    1          certainty, credit and exit protections, and continuing Commission oversight to protect other
    2          customer classes.
    3                 The proposed XLPL tariff and the accompanying Terms and Conditions for Extra
    4          Large Load Customers (“T&CXLLC”) incorporate a comprehensive set of customer
    5          protections that operate at multiple levels to safeguard OG&E’s existing customers from
    6          potential cost shifts associated with serving large load customers, while also establishing
    7          structural protections for OG&E itself against financial exposure from customer default or
    8          early departure. As discussed in detail in the testimony of OG&E witness Cash, these
    9          protections include a 15-year minimum service term with termination and capacity
   10          reduction fees, a CIAC requirement, a collateral requirement, special pricing provisions,
   11          minimum billing demand and energy obligations, and a reservation charge mechanism.
   12                 As explained in the Direct Testimony of Kimber Shoop, adding large loads will
   13          benefit OG&E’s existing customer classes by paying their allocated portion of all existing
   14          shared system costs. Put simply, additional large-load customers with increased usage help
   15          pay the existing costs of the entire system and reduce the average cost to serve each
   16          customer. Existing system costs will be spread over many more kilowatt-hours, resulting
   17          in all customers on the system paying less per kilowatt-hour. The new loads, therefore, put
   18          downward pressure on rates for all customer classes, including residential, commercial,
   19          and industrial customers. For example, in Case No. PUD2026-000031, OG&E witness
   20          Jason Thenmadathil testified about the clear benefit to existing customers of adding
   21          Google’s load to OG&E’s existing cost-of-service study.
   22                 As some intervenors point out, the illustrative analysis is incomplete because it does
   23          not include the currently unknown costs of adding large loads to the system. That is correct,
   24          and it is why OG&E included the additional protections in the XLPL Tariff and Terms and
   25          Conditions: to protect other customer classes from potential incremental cost increases that
   26          could result from serving those large loads. OG&E believes the Commission should resist
   27          proposals that would weaken those protections. I recommend that the Commission approve
   28          them as discussed in this testimony and revisit and refine them in future general rate
   29          proceedings as the associated costs and revenues become known.




        Redacted Rebuttal Testimony of John Laws                                               Page 4 of 29
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 30




    1   Q.     PAO witness Dismukes recommends several modifications intended to align the
    2          XLPL tariff with the PSO settlement tariff and with median terms approved
    3          nationwide. How do you respond generally?
    4   A.     Mr. Dismukes’s survey is a useful contribution to the record, and on most provisions it
    5          supports OG&E’s proposal. He finds that OG&E’s 75 MW threshold equals the national
    6          median, that the 85 percent minimum billing demand is within a normal range, that the 15-
    7          year term and five-year load ramp are consistent with approved tariffs, that an exit fee
    8          based on remaining minimum charges is consistent with other jurisdictions, and that the
    9          CIAC requirement is similar in nature to other tariffs.1
   10                 Where he recommends changes, his principal reference point is the contested
   11          settlement tariff in a PSO case (which is not supported by PSO or the Attorney General).
   12          OG&E would urge caution in treating that tariff as a benchmark.               The ALJ has
   13          recommended approval of the settlement, but PSO, the Attorney General, and other parties
   14          did not join that contested stipulation, and the Commission has yet to act on the
   15          recommendation. Additionally, the contested settlement in the PSO case is uniformly less
   16          protective than OG&E’s proposal; for example, it requires collateral equal to 48 months of
   17          non-fuel minimum bills, which is less than what OG&E is proposing here and interestingly
   18          twice the 24 months Mr. Dismukes recommends.2 A negotiated settlement reflects trade-
   19          offs among its provisions, and selecting individual terms from it without the remainder of
   20          the package does not reproduce the balance the settling parties struck.
   21
   22                        CONTRIBUTION IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
   23   Q.     What does the CIAC requirement accomplish?
   24   A.     The CIAC requirement causes the XLPL customer to fund all transmission and distribution
   25          infrastructure costs dedicated to serve its new or expanded load, plus applicable taxes. This
   26          prevents those customer-caused investments from being placed in rate base and recovered
   27          from other customers.




        1
               Dismukes Responsive, 9:1–3; 10:12–14; 11:14–21; 12:4–6; 14:3–6.
        2
               Dismukes Responsive, Exhibit DED-2.
        Redacted Rebuttal Testimony of John Laws                                               Page 5 of 29
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 30




    1    Q.    Should the tariff expressly state that CIAC-funded infrastructure will not be included
    2          in rate base?
    3    A.    Yes. OG&E does not object to clarifying that amounts funded through CIAC will be
    4          excluded from rate base and will not earn a return. If a facility later provides broader
    5          system benefits, that later use does not place the customer-funded amount into rate base or
    6          create a reimbursement right. Any future system investment not funded through CIAC
    7          would remain subject to the Commission’s ordinary cost-allocation and ratemaking review.
    8
    9    Q.    Some intervenors have testified that the CIAC requirement should be limited to
   10          dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure that is used exclusively by the
   11          XLPL customer. Do you agree with that?
   12    A.    Yes, with an important clarification. Whether CIAC applies should be determined by the
   13          facility’s purpose and cost assignment when it is constructed. An XLPL customer should
   14          pay CIAC for infrastructure constructed specifically to serve that customer. Infrastructure
   15          planned at the outset for broader system use should be allocated under the otherwise
   16          applicable Commission-approved methodology rather than funded through CIAC. If a
   17          CIAC-funded facility later serves additional customers, that later use does not change the
   18          original purpose or cost assignment, place the customer-funded amount into rate base, or
   19          create a reimbursement entitlement. SPP and FERC are exploring how to assign the costs
   20          of new transmission infrastructure needed for large loads, and the Commission should
   21          preserve flexibility to apply future cost-allocation requirements to investments not already
   22          funded through CIAC.
   23
   24    Q.    What additional CIAC recommendations do you address?
   25    A.    Google witness Kimbrough recommends granting customers a right to self-build and self-
   26          finance dedicated facilities; customer audit and reconciliation against as-built invoices
   27          within ninety days of energization with refunds plus interest; express exclusion of
   28          customer-funded assets from rate base; and a reimbursement mechanism where a
   29          subsequent customer uses excess capacity created by an earlier customer’s funded




         Redacted Rebuttal Testimony of John Laws                                             Page 6 of 29
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 68 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 30




    1          upgrade.3 OIEC witness Dauphinais similarly recommends limiting CIAC to transmission
    2          infrastructure that solely serves the XLPL customer or whose costs SPP directly assigns to
    3          OG&E.4 PUD witness Scalf recommends that Section 505 expressly state that CIAC-
    4          funded infrastructure is excluded from rate base.5
    5
    6    Q.    What is OG&E’s position on rate-base exclusion, audit, and refund?
    7    A.    OG&E agrees that all amounts funded through CIAC under the XLPL tariff should be
    8          excluded from rate base and that the Company should neither earn a return on nor seek rate
    9          recovery of those amounts. OG&E does not oppose stating that commitment expressly in
   10          Section 505. Reconciliation and refund are already required by the Preliminary Agreement
   11          and ESA Section 5.03(b). If the customer’s CIAC payment exceeds the final actual cost,
   12          OG&E will refund the overpayment with interest at the customer-deposit rate established
   13          annually by the Commission. OG&E also does not object in principle to a defined review
   14          of the final actual costs of as-built invoices against the customer’s CIAC payment, provided
   15          the reconciliation deadline runs from receipt of final contractor and vendor invoices rather
   16          than energization. That reconciliation does not create a later reimbursement right if a
   17          facility originally dedicated to one customer subsequently serves another customer.
   18
   19    Q.    What is OG&E’s position on customer self-build?
   20    A.    OG&E objects to a customer self-build right. Facilities interconnecting a load of this
   21          magnitude become part of the system OG&E must operate, maintain, and answer for.
   22          OG&E retains responsibility for compliance with Transmission Owner, SPP, and federal
   23          reliability requirements regardless of who constructs the facilities. The evolving reliability
   24          requirements applicable to computational loads further counsel against dividing
   25          construction responsibility.

    1    Q.    Do any responsive witnesses find the 15-year term and five-year load ramp consistent
    2          with other large load tariffs?
    3    A.    Yes. PAO witness Dismukes, whose survey covers thirteen approved large load tariffs,
    4          finds that minimum contract terms range from 8 to 20 years and concludes that OG&E’s
    5          proposed 15-year term is consistent with those results.6 He reaches the same conclusion
    6          regarding the five-year maximum load ramp period.7 Mr. Dismukes does not recommend
    7          a change to either provision.
    8
    9    Q.    What is OG&E’s response to recommendations that reduce the initial term to ten
   10          years?
   11    A.    OG&E does not support reducing the initial term to ten years. HB 2992 establishes ten
   12          years as a statutory floor, not a presumptive term. A 15-year standard term better matches
   13          the planning and capacity commitments required to serve an extra-large load and provides
   14          greater protection against cost shifts to other customers.
   15                   The record supports that balance. Mr. Dismukes finds the 15-year term consistent
   16          with approved tariffs, and Mr. Kimbrough accepts a 15-year initial term for customers
   17          taking full generation and energy supply from OG&E.8
   18
   19    Q.    What changes does Google witness Kimbrough propose regarding contract renewals?
   20    A.    Mr. Kimbrough recommends eliminating the automatic two-year renewal provision,
   21          reducing the non-renewal notice requirement from twenty-four months to twelve months,
   22          and applying the notice requirement symmetrically to both OG&E and the customer.9
   23
   24    Q.    Does OG&E support those recommendations regarding contract renewals?
   25    A.    No. These recommendations seek maximum flexibility for large load customers and fail
   26          to consider the planning requirements of OG&E, which already provided for a symmetrical
   27          notice requirement of both OG&E and the customer and a twelve month non-renewal
   28          notice requirement after the first Renewal Term has commenced. OG&E recommends

    1          retaining the automatic two-year renewal provision and the twenty-four-month non-
    2          renewal notice requirement prior to the end of the Initial Term. Once a Renewal Term has
    3          commenced, the non-renewal notice requirement is reduced to twelve months. Automatic
    4          renewal preserves continuity without imposing another long-term commitment, and
    5          twenty-four months prior to the end of the Initial Term provides a meaningful planning
    6          horizon for generation, transmission, infrastructure, procurement, and future rate design.
    7
    8                     TERMINATION AND CAPACITY-REDUCTION FEES
    9    Q.    Does OG&E believe that the early termination and capacity reduction fees are
   10          appropriate?
   11    A.    Yes. In order to protect other customers from losing the benefits of the large loads and
   12          avoid having to pay for stranded costs that could be incurred in this situation, OG&E’s
   13          T&CXLLC includes fees if an XLPL customer terminates the contract or reduces its
   14          contract demand during the term. First, such a termination or capacity reduction can only
   15          occur after the ninth year and the XLPL customer must give a three-year notice. This
   16          means any termination or capacity reduction can only occur after the 12th year of the Initial
   17          Term. Second, in the case of a capacity reduction, the XLPL customer can only reduce its
   18          contract demand by a maximum of 25 percent. Third, if an XLPL customer terminates or
   19          reduces its contract demand, it will be required to prepay one hundred percent (100%) of
   20          the Minimum Charges for the remainder of the initial contract term impacted by such early
   21          termination or capacity reduction in the form of a one-time fee in order to make any such
   22          election effective. Because an XLPL customer cannot provide the requisite three-year
   23          notice for termination or capacity reduction until year 9 of the Initial Term has been
   24          completed, the amount of Minimum Charges associated with any early termination exit fee
   25          or capacity reduction fee will not exceed three (3) years of Minimum Charges. The ESA
   26          contained in the T&CXLLC also provides that in no event shall any early termination exit
   27          fee or capacity reduction fee be less than one year of Minimum Charges.
   28
   29    Q.    What disputed recommendations do you address in this section?
   30    A.    Google witness Kimbrough accepts the structure of OG&E’s fee but recommends
   31          discounting the remaining minimum charges to net present value and imposing an

    1          affirmative mitigation duty with credits for net revenues from redeployed capacity.10 OIEC
    2          witness Dauphinais recommends a fee based on remaining net plant less residual value,
    3          applicable upon termination or capacity reduction and at the end of the initial term.11 PAO
    4          witness Dismukes recommends ongoing review and potential liquidation of assets built to
    5          serve XLPL customers, with any unrecovered shortfall assigned to the XLPL class.12
    6
    7    Q.    Why does OG&E base the termination and capacity-reduction fees on minimum
    8          charges?
    9    A.    Minimum charges are tied to the obligation the customer accepts when it begins service
   10          and to the capacity OG&E must plan for and stand ready to provide. This approach gives
   11          both parties a transparent amount that can be estimated when the ESA is signed and
   12          administered at departure without an asset-by-asset cost-of-service proceeding. PAO
   13          witness Dismukes likewise finds that an exit fee based on remaining minimum charges is
   14          consistent with large-load tariffs approved in other jurisdictions.13
   15
   16    Q.    Is there common ground on the basic structure of the fee?
   17    A.    On the most fundamental question, yes, and it is worth stating clearly. Mr. Kimbrough
   18          concludes that structuring an exit fee around remaining contractual minimum charges is a
   19          reasonable, practical, and well-established regulatory approach to protect captive
   20          ratepayers from stranded costs, and that tying the fee to the minimum monthly billing
   21          obligations the customer committed to pay establishes a clear, transparent baseline while
   22          avoiding complex, subjective post-departure disputes over individual asset cost
   23          allocations.14
   24                 OG&E agrees with that assessment, and it bears directly on Mr. Dauphinais’s
   25          alternative. The principal large load customer participating in this proceeding — the party
   26          with the most immediate financial interest in a lower exit fee — has examined the

    1          minimum-charges approach and endorsed it over precisely the kind of asset-by-asset
    2          calculation Mr. Dauphinais proposes.
    3
    4    Q.    Please respond to Mr. Kimbrough’s recommendation that the fee be discounted to net
    5          present value.
    6    A.    OG&E understands the time-value principle Mr. Kimbrough invokes and does not dispute
    7          it in the abstract. Our concern is that his recommendation examines the fee in isolation
    8          from the provisions that surround it, and those provisions already moderate the customer’s
    9          obligation substantially.
   10                 A customer cannot give notice until after the ninth Contract Year, must provide
   11          thirty-six months’ notice, and continues taking service under all tariff provisions during
   12          that notice period. The fee itself is then capped—it may not exceed three years of
   13          Minimum Charges, regardless of how much of the Initial Term remains. PUD witness
   14          Scalf makes this point in reviewing Mr. DeCourcey’s comparison table.15
   15                 The practical consequence is that the amount Mr. Kimbrough proposes to discount
   16          is already a moderated figure. Applying a WACC discount on top of an existing cap would
   17          compound two reductions to the same obligation. Moreover, NPV discounting assumes an
   18          economic return on the prepaid amount that does not align with how OG&E would hold
   19          and apply the proceeds over the remaining contract period. The resulting fee therefore
   20          could fall materially below the fixed costs OG&E continues to carry after the customer
   21          departs and leave OG&E customers with a funding shortfall relative to the original
   22          contractual bargain.
   23
   24    Q.    Does the cap create the very risk Mr. Dauphinais identifies?
   25    A.    It does, and I would acknowledge that his criticism and Mr. Kimbrough’s recommendation
   26          point in opposite directions on the same provision. Mr. Dauphinais observes that a capped
   27          fee may understate actual stranded costs, particularly because production and transmission
   28          assets have depreciable lives well in excess of the term.16 That is a legitimate observation

    1          about where the cap places residual risk — with OG&E and, ultimately, with other
    2          customers.
    3                 OG&E accepted that cap as a reasonable balance between customer protection and
    4          commercial workability. But a provision already calibrated in the customer’s favor is not
    5          a sound candidate for further reduction.
    6
    7    Q.    Please respond to Mr. Kimbrough’s proposed duty to mitigate.
    8    A.    OG&E opposes imposing an affirmative duty to mitigate or providing a credit based on
    9          alleged redeployment of capacity. The filed fee is a clear contractual obligation based on
   10          the customer’s remaining minimum charges, which reflect the recovery of fixed costs that
   11          have been made to provide service to the XLPL customers for the full contract term, not a
   12          windfall to the utility or its other customers. Requiring mitigation would convert that
   13          known obligation into an uncertain amount dependent on events, ripe for dispute, occurring
   14          after the customer’s departure.
   15                 Mr. Kimbrough’s own rationale for the minimum-charges approach is that it avoids
   16          complex, subjective post-departure disputes over individual asset cost allocations. A
   17          mitigation credit would reintroduce that complexity through a different route. The parties
   18          would dispute what capacity was released, whether it was actually redeployed, what
   19          revenues and incremental costs are attributable to replacement service, whether
   20          replacement load would have materialized regardless, and how market revenues over a
   21          multi-year period should be measured.
   22                 PUD witness Scalf’s proposed Protocol illustrates rather than resolves the problem.
   23          Section 515.13 would require determinations regarding the remaining net cost of released
   24          capacity, the price obtained from alleged redeployment, and whether capacity was
   25          separately procured for a replacement customer.17 Those fact-intensive determinations
   26          would invite the same post-departure disputes the filed minimum-charges approach is
   27          designed to avoid. OG&E therefore recommends approval of the fee as filed, without a
   28          mitigation duty or redeployment credit.




         17
               Scalf Responsive Exhibit DS-3 § 515.13.

    1    Q.    Please respond to Mr. Dauphinais’s remaining net plant approach.
    2    A.    Mr. Dauphinais introduces another exit fee concept — a fee equal to remaining net plant
    3          less residual value would, as he says, match the stranded costs at the moment of departure.
    4          OG&E’s difficulty is that the calculation depends on inputs that cannot be determined
    5          objectively at the time they would be needed.
    6                 There are three difficulties with this concept in particular. First, identifying which
    7          production investments were made to serve a given customer is contested even in the
    8          abstract; Mr. Beling explains that because resource needs are driven by multiple factors
    9          and commercial operation dates rarely coincide with a new load’s start, it is very difficult
   10          to specifically identify which resources should be considered incremental to a new large
   11          load.18 Second, estimating residual value to other customers at a future date requires
   12          assumptions about load growth, market conditions, and accreditation that will themselves
   13          likely be disputed. Third, Mr. Dauphinais proposes that the resulting figure be subject to
   14          Commission review — which means the exit fee would not be known until after a
   15          proceeding concluded, potentially years after the customer gave notice.19
   16                 The result would be a fee that is conceptually elegant but commercially
   17          indeterminate. Neither OG&E nor the customer could quantify the obligation in advance,
   18          and the collateral requirement — presently sized against known Minimum Charges —
   19          would have no relevant reference point.
   20
